paragraphs: The paper asks how the brain represents locations when information comes from several senses and must guide movement. Vision, hearing, and touch encode position relative to different reference points. Combining these signals therefore requires transformations between representations, and the abstract emphasizes that these transformations become complicated when locations are encoded across populations of neurons.

The authors argue that the spatial tasks they study require intermediate representations that do not stay invariant within one reference frame. They introduce an iterative basis function map using units whose responses are modulated by posture or whose spatial sensitivity shifts partially. These properties connect the proposed computation to the kinds of responses observed outside primary sensory cortex.

The map is presented as performing sensory prediction, multisensory integration, sensory-to-movement transformations, and motor control optimally within the proposed formulation. The authors also test it against neurophysiological and neuropsychological data. Its central contribution is a computational account of why mixed spatial representations can support coordinated spatial behavior.
neurips-2000-a-new-model-of-spatial-repr.tldr: An iterative neural map uses mixed spatial representations to combine sensory information and guide movement.

paragraphs: Training a linear support vector machine involves an optimization problem whose size can become substantial when there are many examples. This paper develops a new algorithm by applying an active set strategy to the dual of a reformulated version of that problem. The resulting procedure solves a finite sequence of systems of linear equations.

Those systems would ordinarily have a dimension tied to the number of training points. The key computational step uses the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula to replace the large matrix inversion with an inversion whose size is tied to the input dimension. This changes which aspect of the dataset determines the matrix size at each step.

The reported example contains seven million points with 32 input dimensions. Training requires inversions of symmetric positive definite matrices measuring 33 by 33 and takes 96 minutes on a 400 MHz Pentium II. The implementation needs an available linear equation solver rather than specialized quadratic or linear programming software. This demonstrates the approach's practicality for the reported large, low-dimensional problem.
neurips-2000-active-support-vector-machi.tldr: A reformulated linear SVM algorithm handles millions of examples by solving systems whose matrix size follows the input dimension.

paragraphs: This paper examines how stripe-like patterns can develop in a model of cortical organization. Its setting is ocular dominance, and its focus is the theoretical behavior of a particular model for one-dimensional pattern formation. The authors begin from the widespread use of Hebbian and competitive Hebbian learning in accounts of cortical development.

The analysis brings together two sets of modeling choices. One concerns competitive and interactive influences within the cortex. The other concerns initial arborization: the starting arrangement of neural branches and connections, considered under both free and restricted conditions. Treating these choices within a common framework makes their roles part of the same theoretical problem.

The contribution described is a detailed analysis of an adapted model, with these influences placed on comparable terms. Its significance lies in connecting the learning interactions that shape a developing pattern with the initial connection structure on which those interactions act. The stated scope is the one-dimensional stripe model, providing a focused setting for studying these ingredients together.
neurips-2000-competition-and-arbors-in-o.tldr: A theoretical model brings cortical competition, interaction, and initial connection structure into one account of stripe formation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to simplify reinforcement learning for deciding whether a communications link should admit incoming calls. The traffic follows a self-similar arrival process, and the proposed technique, predictive gain scheduling, divides the control problem into parts. Its purpose is to make learning easier while preserving the quality of admission decisions.

One part predicts call arrival rates in the near future while the system is operating. Another prepares control policies in advance for Poisson arrival processes. At each decision, the predicted arrival rate determines which prepared policy to use. Prediction therefore connects the changing traffic conditions to a collection of policies computed for simpler arrival models.

Simulations compare this decomposition with a reinforcement learning controller that handles the problem without separating it into those components. The authors report significantly faster learning without a loss in performance in that comparison. The result supports using prediction to select among prepared policies as a useful simplification for the admission-control problem studied.
neurips-2000-decomposition-of-reinforcem.tldr: Predicting arrival rates and selecting precomputed policies speeds up learning without performance loss in the reported admission-control simulations.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks underlying independent sources in observed data. This paper proposes a Bayesian framework for that task using ensemble learning and linear response theory from statistical physics. The framework is applied to both discrete and continuous sources, giving the authors a common approach across different kinds of hidden signals.

For continuous sources, the paper examines the underdetermined case, where there are more sources than observed mixtures. The authors report that a naive mean-field approximation fails in this setting. Linear response theory improves the covariance estimates and is described as very efficient, making the treatment of relationships among uncertain quantities a central part of the method.

The examples use sources without temporal correlations. The authors state that the derivation can readily be extended to include such correlations, distinguishing that proposed extension from the examples actually presented. They also explain that the framework offers a straightforward route to new ICA algorithms without explicitly specifying the source prior distribution.
neurips-2000-ensemble-learning-and-linea.tldr: A Bayesian ICA framework uses linear response theory to improve covariance estimates where naive mean-field inference fails.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional structure from images requires deciding which measurements in different images refer to the same features. The paper identifies this correspondence problem as a major obstacle. Tracking-based approaches assume features remain traceable across frames, while the rigidity-based matching methods discussed in the abstract work only under restricted camera motion.

The proposed Bayesian approach considers a distribution over possible correspondences. This preserves uncertainty about ambiguous matches instead of making an early commitment to a single preferred assignment. The paper develops both a fully Bayesian treatment, which produces a posterior distribution, and a maximum a posteriori treatment, which uses expectation–maximization to maximize that posterior.

Markov chain Monte Carlo provides a practical way to implement these treatments, and the authors present experiments on real data. The contribution is both representational and computational: correspondence uncertainty becomes part of the inference problem, and sampling makes the proposed inference procedures usable. The two treatments offer different ways to work with the same underlying uncertainty.
neurips-2000-feature-correspondence-a-ma.tldr: Bayesian correspondence inference uses Monte Carlo methods to account for uncertain image matches during 3D reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper connects three properties of a learned classifier: how many mistakes a learning algorithm makes, how sparsely its result can be represented, and how well it may generalize. The starting point is an improvement to Novikoff's perceptron convergence theorem. The authors reinterpret the resulting mistake bound as a guarantee about sparsity that depends on the classification margin.

That reinterpretation supports a PAC-style bound on the generalization error of the classifier produced by the perceptron. A crucial feature is that the bound depends on the margin a support vector machine would obtain using the same dataset and kernel. The support vector solution thus supplies a reference quantity for analyzing the perceptron's classifier.

The authors report that this bound gives stronger guarantees than those then available for the support vector solution itself. This is a comparison of theoretical guarantees, rather than a claim that the perceptron always predicts more accurately. The contribution shows how a margin-based analysis can yield a sparsity-based route to generalization guarantees.
neurips-2000-from-margin-to-sparsity-623.tldr: An improved perceptron mistake bound becomes a margin-dependent sparsity guarantee and then a generalization-error bound.

paragraphs: The paper examines datasets with more measured dimensions than examples. In this setting, the training examples do not fully span the signal space. The authors identify a resulting bias: variance measured along directions chosen from the training data is too large compared with the average variance of independent test examples projected onto those same directions.

This matters when singular value decomposition is used to summarize the data before fitting another statistical model. The training-derived directions come with estimates of how much variation they explain, and those estimates can be misleading for new examples. Generalizable Singular Value Decomposition, or GenSVD, addresses the problem by re-estimating the singular values obtained from conventional SVD.

The intended effect is to reduce this variance bias and allow a subsequent model to generalize better. The authors demonstrate successful bias correction on data from a functional PET study of human brain activation. The contribution is therefore a correction to the statistical quantities attached to an SVD representation, motivated by their behavior on independent data.
neurips-2000-generalizable-singular-valu.tldr: GenSVD re-estimates singular values to reduce inflated training-variance estimates in datasets with more dimensions than examples.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Interactive Parts model as an alternative to hidden Markov models for recognizing online cursive handwriting. Both approaches are tested on a database of cursive script. The comparison focuses on recognition behavior and on the computational consequences of modeling how long individual parts of the writing extend.

Under the assumption that every letter has the same average width, the tested implementations produce comparable results. That assumption is important to the reported comparison: it specifies the setting in which the two models perform similarly. The abstract therefore supports comparable recognition under that shared condition, rather than a general claim that one model recognizes handwriting better.

The distinguishing capability is duration modeling. The authors state that the Interactive Parts model can include it without increasing computational complexity, in contrast to HMMs. This makes the contribution about the cost of representing duration as well as recognition itself. The model offers a way to accommodate that aspect of cursive script while retaining the stated computational complexity.
neurips-2000-interactive-parts-model-an-.tldr: Interactive Parts matches HMM recognition under a shared letter-width assumption while supporting duration modeling without added computational complexity.

paragraphs: The paper addresses instability in reinforcement learning methods that combine temporal-difference learning with neural networks or other parametric value-function approximators. Such methods estimate the value of decisions in a Markov decision process, but the abstract notes that their learning procedures are frequently unstable. The authors introduce a kernel-based approach to overcome this difficulty.

The method is developed for an average-cost formulation, where the objective concerns costs over continued operation. The authors prove convergence to a unique solution. This supplies a definite mathematical endpoint for the learning procedure and directly addresses the stability problem that motivates the work.

They also establish consistency: the costs produced by the method approach optimal costs asymptotically. This is a separate claim from convergence to a unique solution, because it connects the limiting behavior to the control objective. Optimal portfolio choice provides the practical application. The stated contribution combines a stable learning procedure with an asymptotic guarantee about the quality of its resulting costs.
neurips-2000-kernel-based-reinforcement-.tldr: A kernel-based average-cost reinforcement learning method has a unique convergence limit and asymptotically optimal costs.

paragraphs: This paper learns a statistical description of repeating human movements and uses it to support tracking in video. The training material is a large collection of three-dimensional periodic motion. The method automatically divides these recordings into cycles, making repeated portions of an activity the units from which the motion model is built.

The authors then compute an average cycle and principal components describing variation among cycles. Their algorithm accounts for missing information and enforces smooth transitions between cycles. These features connect the statistical representation to the temporal structure of motion: the learned description must accommodate incomplete observations while allowing successive cycles to join smoothly.

The resulting temporal model supplies prior probabilities over possible human motions. Within a Bayesian tracking framework, that prior can guide interpretation of complex video recorded by a single camera and support recovery of three-dimensional movement. The approach matters because information learned from repeated 3D activities becomes a structured source of guidance for interpreting motion in monocular images.
neurips-2000-learning-and-tracking-cycli.tldr: A learned model of smooth motion cycles supplies a Bayesian prior for tracking people and recovering 3D movement from single-camera video.

paragraphs: Human motion changes over time in ways that are both nonlinear and varied. This paper models that behavior with switching linear dynamic systems learned from motion-capture data. The approach represents motion through linear dynamics together with switches between them, providing a way to describe richer behavior than a single linear system could express.

The authors present results for generating motion, classifying it, and tracking it visually. A central computational obstacle is that exact inference in the switching model is intractable. They therefore introduce three approximate inference algorithms and compare their performance. One is a new variational algorithm derived by expressing the switching system as a dynamic Bayesian network.

In the reported classification experiments, switching linear models outperform conventional hidden Markov models for the human-motion domain studied. The finding supports the usefulness of the model in that setting. The work combines a representation of changing motion dynamics with practical inference methods, connecting the model's expressive structure to several motion-processing tasks.
neurips-2000-learning-switching-linear-m.tldr: Switching linear models learned from motion capture support synthesis, tracking, and classification, outperforming conventional HMMs in the reported classification experiments.

paragraphs: The paper presents directions for speech recognition that divide the speech signal among multiple processing streams. These multi-stream and multi-band approaches extend recognition based on hidden Markov models. Different experts process different channels or characteristics of the signal, allowing the overall system to combine several specialized views of the same speech.

In the described formulation, the experts are treated as independent. Their likelihoods or posterior probabilities are combined at a temporal stage to produce the final recognition output. The organization of this combination is central: recognition depends on how information from the separate streams is brought together, as well as on what each expert detects.

The authors then introduce HMM2 as a further extension. Here, each state's emission probabilities are estimated using feature-based HMMs specific to that state. These additional models merge stream information and represent possible correlations between streams. The contribution is an architectural progression from separate experts to a structured mechanism for combining their information within an HMM-based recognizer.
neurips-2000-new-approaches-towards-robu.tldr: Multi-stream speech recognition combines specialized signal experts, while HMM2 uses state-specific HMMs to merge streams and model their correlations.

paragraphs: The paper establishes a connection between kernel principal component analysis and metric multidimensional scaling. Both provide ways to construct a representation of data, but the connection shown here has a specific condition: the kernel must be isotropic. In this setting, its value depends only on the distance between two input points.

Under that condition, the authors show that kernel PCA can be interpreted as a form of metric multidimensional scaling. This connects a kernel-based analysis to the task of arranging points according to their distance relationships. The condition matters because the stated interpretation is tied to distance-dependent kernels, rather than being asserted for every possible kernel function.

The connection yields a metric multidimensional scaling algorithm that obtains its point configuration by solving an eigenproblem. It replaces iterative optimization of a stress objective with that spectral calculation. The paper also discusses kernel choice, linking the choice of similarity function to the resulting representation. Its contribution is both a conceptual equivalence and an associated computational route.
neurips-2000-on-a-connection-between-ker.tldr: With an isotropic kernel, kernel PCA becomes a form of metric multidimensional scaling solved through an eigenproblem.

paragraphs: This paper studies which stable activity patterns can occur in symmetric threshold-linear neural networks. The authors analyze subnetworks made up of neurons that are active together. This local linear analysis determines the stability of candidate steady states and provides information beyond what the energy-function and Lyapunov approaches discussed in the abstract reveal.

The stability analysis identifies two kinds of eigenmodes. One governs global stability; the other determines whether multiple stable states are possible. The authors also prove equivalence between their stability criteria and criteria from quadratic programming. This connects the behavior of a recurrent neural circuit to a mathematical optimization framework.

The analysis separates neuron groups into permitted sets, which can be active together at a steady state, and forbidden sets, which cannot. Every subset of a permitted set is permitted, while every superset of a forbidden set remains forbidden. Interpreting permitted sets as stored memories yields a broader formulation of long-term memory than the traditional account based on individual fixed-point attractors.
neurips-2000-permitted-and-forbidden-set.tldr: Stability analysis identifies which neuron groups can coexist at steady states and supports a broader account of stored memories.

paragraphs: The paper builds a model of place cells and head-direction cells by combining visual information with proprioceptive signals about the robot's own movement. The aim is to connect a representation of location and direction with goal-oriented navigation. A miniature robot supplies the visual input through an onboard video camera.

The images are processed with Gabor filters at 31 nodes arranged in a log-polar retinotopic graph. Unsupervised Hebbian learning then incrementally forms a population of localized, overlapping place fields. In this representation, different cells respond to different regions, and their overlapping responses provide a population-based description of the robot's location.

Those place cells serve as basis functions for reinforcement learning, linking the learned spatial representation to navigation decisions. The authors present experimental results for a mobile robot navigating toward goals. The contribution is the integration of visual preprocessing, self-motion information, learned place fields, and reinforcement learning into a single navigation model, with the spatial code supplying the representation used for learning.
neurips-2000-place-cells-and-spatial-nav.tldr: A robot combines vision and self-motion signals to learn place fields that support reinforcement learning for navigation.

paragraphs: Visual stimuli do not always land at precisely the same retinal position, even when a task asks a person to maintain fixation. This paper examines how that positional variability changes perceptual discrimination. The authors argue that inference with varying positions has a different computational structure from inference about stimuli presented at a fixed position.

Specifically, the analysis introduces a quadratic nonlinearity where purely linear discrimination would otherwise be considered. The authors show that accounting for this nonlinearity benefits discrimination and demonstrate better performance with a recurrent network. They suggest that recurrent connections in primary visual cortex could serve this computational role.

The paper also proposes a connection to the different speeds observed in perceptual learning. Learning feedforward connections is associated with the fast component, while learning recurrent connections is associated with the slow component. This remains a proposed interpretation of those learning components. Together, the results connect unavoidable position variation, nonlinear discrimination, and a possible function for recurrent cortical processing.
neurips-2000-position-variance-recurrenc.tldr: Retinal position variability motivates quadratic discrimination and a proposed role for recurrent connections in perceptual learning.

paragraphs: This paper approaches face recognition by learning a generative model of pairs of images showing the same person. To identify a test image, the method pairs it with images of known identity and chooses the pair with the highest relative probability. Recognition therefore depends on how well a candidate pair fits the learned model.

The model contains one layer of nonlinear, rate-coded feature detectors. Given an observed data vector, the exact posterior distribution over their activities can be inferred quickly, without iterative computation or approximation. This property makes the hidden-feature inference step particularly direct within the proposed architecture.

Learning compares pixel–feature correlations in two phases: one while observing real images, and another while observing reconstructions generated from feature activity. The difference between these phases supplies the basis for adjusting detector weights. The authors describe the learning algorithm as unsupervised and report favorable comparisons with methods in the literature. The contribution combines pair-based recognition with a generative model whose feature inference is exact and rapid.
neurips-2000-rate-coded-restricted-boltz.tldr: A generative model recognizes faces by scoring same-person image pairs and permits rapid, exact inference of hidden feature activities.

paragraphs: The paper studies kernel functions whose value depends on the dot product of their two inputs. Its central question is when such a function satisfies Mercer's condition, making it suitable for use in support vector machines, regularization networks, or Gaussian processes. The authors provide necessary and sufficient conditions for this class of kernels.

For an analytic kernel, which can be expressed as a Taylor series, the paper identifies nonnegativity of every expansion coefficient as a requirement. This translates the validity question into a condition on the coefficients defining the function. It gives a concrete mathematical restriction on candidate dot-product kernels.

The authors also calculate eigenfunctions and eigenvalues to obtain an explicit form of the feature map. This connects the kernel's numerical similarity calculation with the feature representation it implies. The contribution therefore goes beyond deciding whether a kernel is admissible: it also describes the representation underlying it, linking kernel design, spectral structure, and the learning methods that can use it.
neurips-2000-regularization-with-dot-pro.tldr: The paper characterizes valid dot-product kernels and derives explicit feature maps from their eigenfunctions and eigenvalues.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes objects by comparing their shapes with stored examples. The main challenge is finding which points on one shape correspond to points on another. Its proposed descriptor, the shape context, characterizes a point using the distribution of the other shape points relative to it.

Each descriptor is attached to one point but summarizes information about the shape as a whole. The authors show that this makes point correspondences substantially easier to recover. After aligning the shapes, they use shape contexts to calculate a robust similarity score, connecting point matching to the final decision about which shapes resemble one another.

That score is used in a nearest-neighbor classifier for both handwritten digits and three-dimensional objects, with the same distance function in both applications. On MNIST, the reported error rate is 0.63%, outperforming other published techniques in the paper's comparison. The contribution is a descriptor that supports correspondence, alignment, and recognition within one shape-matching approach.
neurips-2000-shape-context-a-new-descrip.tldr: Shape contexts summarize surrounding shape points to simplify matching and achieve a reported 0.63% MNIST error with nearest-neighbor recognition.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis extends ordinary PCA by using a kernel to define an implicit nonlinear feature space. Standard PCA is then performed in that space. The paper addresses a representation problem with this method: each resulting component depends on kernel evaluations associated with every training example.

The authors propose approximating the feature-space covariance matrix using a smaller collection of example vectors. They choose this approximation through a maximum-likelihood approach. Because the covariance matrix determines the principal components, changing its representation provides a route to components that depend on far fewer example vectors.

The paper reports that this can produce a highly sparse version of kernel PCA without losing effectiveness. Here, sparsity concerns the number of examples needed to express the components, rather than the number of original input coordinates. The contribution preserves the nonlinear feature-space approach while reducing its dependence on the complete training set, directly addressing the source of the original method's dense representation.
neurips-2000-sparse-kernel-principal-com.tldr: A maximum-likelihood covariance approximation can make kernel PCA highly sparse without loss of effectiveness.

paragraphs: The paper extends a theoretical link between the number of support vectors and expected generalization error. The original result bounds expected error by the expected fraction of training examples that are support vectors. The extension covers a broad class of kernel machines, including soft-margin support vector classification, regression, and regularization networks.

The authors then replace classification error with margin error, defined here as an example receiving positive cost. Under that change, key inequalities become equalities. In particular, the expected true margin error equals the expected empirical margin error. These statements concern expectations, so they do not assert that the corresponding errors coincide for every individual training sample.

A further result gives a necessary condition for sparse solutions: the cost function must be partially insensitive. The claim does not say that this property alone guarantees sparsity. Together, the results connect the way a learning objective assigns cost with the possibility of a compact data representation and with theoretical error relationships.
neurips-2000-sparsity-of-data-representa.tldr: The paper extends support-vector error results to broader kernel machines and shows partial cost insensitivity is necessary for sparse solutions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a staged approach to error-correcting codes and image restoration. Its central idea is to extract information from an earlier processing stage and pass selected information to a later stage. The later stage uses that information to improve its result, making the relationship between stages part of the processing method.

Selectivity is an explicit feature of the proposal. The information obtained earlier is used selectively to help the subsequent stage, rather than simply treating the first result as the final answer. In both application areas, this creates a mechanism for an intermediate result to contribute to further recovery or correction.

The authors study the approach using mean-field analysis based on the cavity method and through simulations. Both support an advantage in robustness when hyperparameter estimates are uncertain. That finding matters because the stated benefit concerns sensitivity to parameter estimation, alongside performance improvement across stages. The contribution is a shared processing strategy for the two tasks, supported by both theoretical analysis and simulation evidence.
neurips-2000-stagewise-processing-in-err.tldr: Selectively reusing information across processing stages improves robustness to uncertain hyperparameter estimates in coding and image restoration.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a basic problem in cognitive science: how to choose among computational explanations when observations are limited. Several models may offer accounts of the same cognitive process, so comparing them requires a selection principle. The authors introduce Minimum Description Length, or MDL, for making this choice among computational models of cognition.

A second contribution concerns understanding the selection principle itself. The authors use differential geometry to give an intuitive account of what drives MDL's decisions. This connects the formal model-selection method to a way of interpreting why it favors one candidate explanation over another, making the basis for selection part of the paper's focus.

The authors demonstrate the adequacy of MDL in two areas of cognitive modeling. These applications support its use in the settings examined. The work therefore combines a proposed selection method, an interpretation of its behavior, and demonstrations of its applicability, all directed at the problem of comparing explanations from limited observations.
neurips-2000-the-use-of-mdl-to-select-am.tldr: The paper introduces MDL for cognitive-model selection, explains its behavior geometrically, and demonstrates it in two modeling areas.

paragraphs: The paper presents Vicinal Risk Minimization as a framework connecting generative models with methods based on structural risk minimization and statistical regularization. Its aim is to bring approaches usually discussed separately into a shared formulation. Support vector machines are one of the central examples on the regularization side of that connection.

The framework incorporates several existing algorithms, including Parzen windows, support vector machines, ridge regression, constrained logistic classifiers, and Tangent-Prop. Showing how these methods fit together gives the principle a unifying role. It also provides a basis for deriving additional algorithms, extending the contribution beyond a reinterpretation of existing techniques.

The new algorithms address pattern-recognition problems involving very different pattern distributions and problems involving unlabeled data, tasks the abstract associates with generative modeling. The authors present preliminary empirical results. The stated evidence therefore supports an initial investigation of these algorithms, while the broader contribution is a framework that links established methods and generates approaches to additional learning problems.
neurips-2000-vicinal-risk-minimization-9.tldr: Vicinal Risk Minimization unifies several learning methods and yields new algorithms for differing pattern distributions and unlabeled data.
